# Jeremiah 51:44–64 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 44 — *"I will punish Bel in Babylon. I will make him spew out what he swallowed. The nations will no longer stream to him; even the wall of Babylon will fall."*

**Traditional reading:** "Bel" (equivalent to the Canaanite Baal) is the Babylonian chief deity, also called Merodach/Marduk, the patron god of Babylon. God declares that Bel will be "punished" — not that God is angry at a lifeless statue, but that when Babylon falls, her god is seen as powerless and disgraced (Ellicott). The phrase "spew out what he swallowed" refers to the spoils and tribute that Babylon (personified in Bel) devoured from conquered nations — including the temple vessels from Jerusalem (Daniel 5:2; Ezra 1:7). Gill notes that Bel is made to "disgorge his spoil," including the sacred vessels taken from the LORD's house and deposited in Bel's temple, restored under Cyrus. The "wall of Babylon shall fall": Ellicott observes that Babylon's two great walls bore names consecrated to Bel — *Imgur-Bel* ("Bel protects") and *Nimetti-Bel* ("dwelling of Bel") — so the wall's fall is specifically a judgment on Bel's inability to protect. (Pulpit Commentary notes the Septuagint omits from this clause through to the first half of v. 49.)

**Sources:**  
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/51.htm  
- Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/51.htm  
- Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/51-44.htm  
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-51.html

**Methodist (Clarke):** Adam Clarke identifies "what he hath swallowed up" specifically as "the sacred vessels of the temple of Jerusalem, which were taken thence by Nebuchadnezzar, and dedicated to him in his temple at Babylon." The wall "shall cease to be a defence; and shall moulder away until, in process of time, it shall not be discernible." — Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Bel is "the representative god of Babylon," and his punishment means the nation is forced to give back what it seized. "Even the wall of Babylon has fallen" looks toward partial literal fulfillment under Medo-Persia, with an ultimate fulfillment in the fall of "Babylon the Great" in Revelation 17–18. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-51/

---

## v. 45 — *"Come out of her, My people! Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD."*

**Traditional reading:** This is a command to the exiles in Babylon not to settle permanently or put their trust in a city destined for judgment. Matthew Henry calls it a "helpful call to God's people in exile, that they should not put their trust, confidence, and resources into a kingdom that would be judged and conquered." The imperative echoes Genesis 19:12-16 (Lot called out of Sodom) and is applied in Revelation 18:4 to God's people regarding "mystical Babylon."

**Sources:**  
- Matthew Henry: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html  
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-51.html

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** "Again the Lord calls upon His people to flee from Babylon, thus escaping his fierce indignation and saving their own lives" — parallel to Acts 2:40 ("Save yourselves from this corrupt generation"). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 46 — *"Do not let your heart grow faint, and do not be afraid when the rumor is heard in the land; for a rumor will come one year—and then another the next year—of violence in the land and of ruler against ruler."*

**Traditional reading:** God warns His people not to panic at reports of political upheaval and war. Wars and rumours of wars would come in succession ("one year…and then another the next year"), but these are signs of God's unfolding judgment, not causes for terror among His own. The phrase "ruler against ruler" indicates internal strife and coups within Babylon's leadership. Constable notes the purpose is to give God's people advance confidence when they hear such reports.

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke specifies that a rumour of war would come a year before the capture of the city — in that year Cyrus defeated Belshazzar in the field, and the following year the city itself fell. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** "They must not be discouraged, or faint-hearted, because of the political intrigue and violence in the land — when ruler is against ruler!" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 47 — *"Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the idols of Babylon. Her entire land will suffer shame, and all her slain will lie fallen within her."*

**Traditional reading:** The idols of Babylon — including Bel, Nebo, and the host of Babylonian deities — will be shown utterly powerless. "Her entire land will suffer shame" means public humiliation for a nation that boasted of its gods. "All her slain will lie fallen within her" echoes the judgment language of the prior chapter (Jeremiah 50:30). Matthew Henry frames this as God's direct assault on Babylon's religious pride: the very things they trusted in will be exposed as worthless.

**Reformed (Matthew Henry):** The judgment on the graven images shows that God "will convince those by his judgments who would not be convinced by his word." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 48 — *"Then heaven and earth and all that is in them will shout for joy over Babylon because the destroyers from the north will come against her," declares the LORD.*

**Traditional reading:** The fall of Babylon is so just and welcome that creation itself rejoices. Ellicott explains the "destroyers from the north" as the Medo-Persian forces. Constable draws the parallel to Revelation 16:19. The rejoicing of heaven and earth over Babylon is a theme picked up in Revelation 18:20: "Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets."

**Pentecostal (Enduring Word):** "The righteous rejoice – even singing with joy – over the justice and judgments of God." Guzik connects this to both the immediate historical judgment and the eschatological one in Revelation 17–18. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-51/

---

## v. 49 — *"Babylon must fall on account of the slain of Israel, just as the slain of all the earth have fallen because of Babylon."*

**Traditional reading:** Babylon's destruction is retribution for the blood of Israelites she has shed, just as many nations' slain fell because of Babylon's aggression. Ellicott and Constable note the text is difficult. Driver renders it: "Yea, Babylon must fall, O ye slain of Israel; yea, for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth." (Peake's Commentary). The Septuagint omits 44b–49a.

**Modern scholarship (Peake's):** The text is "doubtful" and should be rendered with Driver's translation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 50 — *"You who have escaped the sword, depart and do not linger! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind."*

**Traditional reading:** Addressed to the surviving Jewish exiles. "Remember the LORD from far away" means to turn their hearts back to God even while in distant Babylon. "Let Jerusalem come to mind" is a call to long for Jerusalem and to return there when the opportunity comes. Matthew Henry interprets "remember" as entailing active return, not mere recollection.

**Methodist (Clarke):** Specifically addresses "the Jews" — "Pray for its restoration; and embrace the first opportunity offered of returning thither." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** "Again the Jews are urged to remember and return to Jerusalem (Psalm 137:6) — fleeing the calamity that is about to fall upon the city of pride." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 51 — *"We are ashamed because we have heard reproach; disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD's house."*

**Traditional reading:** This is a communal lament, expressing the deep shame of the exiles upon hearing that pagan Babylonians (or later, other foreigners) have entered and desecrated the temple. Constable connects this to the report in Nehemiah 1:3. The holy places ("sanctuaries" plural) refer to the various courts and chambers of Solomon's temple. The shame reflects not only national humiliation but a realization that their own sin led to this.

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** The reproach and shame are the exiles' confession that the temple's defilement is the direct result of God's judgment on their sin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 52 — *"Therefore, behold, the days are coming," declares the LORD, "when I will punish her idols, and throughout her land the wounded will groan."*

**Traditional reading:** A repetition and reinforcement of v. 47 — the punishment of Babylon's idols is certain. "The wounded will groan" paints the aftermath of battle: not a swift death for all but the groaning of the mortally wounded across the land.

---

## v. 53 — *"Even if Babylon ascends to the heavens and fortifies her lofty stronghold, the destroyers I send will come against her," declares the LORD.*

**Traditional reading:** Hyperbolic language for Babylon's proud self-exaltation. Constable links this to the Babylonian ziggurats (temple towers) designed to reach toward heaven, and to the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1-9). No human fortification — however high — can keep God's judgment out. Isaiah 14:12-14 is a close parallel.

**Methodist (Clarke):** "Though it were fortified even to the skies, it shall fall by the enemies that I will send against it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 54 — *"The sound of a cry comes from Babylon, the sound of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!"*

**Traditional reading:** The prophet hears in advance the cries of anguish at Babylon's fall. This is a dramatic shift to present-tense description — the destruction is so certain that it's already heard. Constable notes that the cries of destruction will replace the loud noise of Babylon's bustling commercial life (cf. Revelation 18:22-23).

---

## v. 55 — *"For the LORD will destroy Babylon; He will silence her mighty voice. The waves will roar like great waters; the tumult of their voices will resound."*

**Traditional reading:** "Her mighty voice" refers to Babylon's arrogant boasting and the noise of her busy commerce and revelry. The "waves" that "roar like great waters" are the invading armies — a metaphor used earlier in the chapter (v. 42: "the sea has come up over Babylon").

**Methodist (Clarke):** "The great voice" is specifically "its pride and insufferable boasting." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 56 — *"For a destroyer is coming against her—against Babylon. Her warriors will be captured, and their bows will be broken, for the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full."*

**Traditional reading:** The "destroyer" (singular) personifies the invading force. Breaking bows signals the shattering of military power. The core theological statement — "the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full" — affirms that Babylon's fall is not random history but divine justice.

**Methodist (Clarke):** "The fall of Babylon is an act of Divine justice; whatever it suffers, it is in consequence of its crimes." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** "The Lord God of recompences, the God to whom vengeance belongs, will surely requite; he will pay them home; he will render unto Babylon all the evil they have done in Zion." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 57 — *"I will make her princes and wise men drunk, along with her governors, officials, and warriors. Then they will fall asleep forever and not wake up," declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts.*

**Traditional reading:** This literally and figuratively describes Babylon's fall. Historical fulfillment came at Belshazzar's drunken feast (Daniel 5), where the king and his nobles drank wine from the temple vessels on the very night the city fell. "Sleep a perpetual sleep" means death. Matthew Henry and Clarke both note this was fulfilled the night Babylon was taken: "many had retired to rest, and never awoke; slain in their beds, they slept a perpetual sleep" (Clarke). The title "the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts" is a majestic assertion of God's sovereignty over all earthly kings.

**Methodist (Clarke):** Links the "feast" to the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5:1-3), possibly a feast in honour of the goddess Sheshach. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 58 — *"This is what the LORD of Hosts says: 'Babylon's thick walls will be leveled, and her high gates consumed by fire. So the labor of the people will be for nothing; the nations will exhaust themselves to fuel the flames.'"*

**Traditional reading:** Herodotus described Babylon's walls as approximately 50 cubits (about 85–100 feet) thick and 200 cubits high, with 25 brazen gates on each side. Yet these would be leveled and burned. "The labour of the people will be for nothing" means that the captive nations who toiled to build Babylon's defenses laboured in vain — their work literally went up in flames. Constable connects this to Habakkuk 2:13 — "the peoples weary themselves for nothing."

**Methodist (Clarke):** Quotes Herodotus on the walls' dimensions and notes: "Had not Cyrus resorted to stratagem, humanly speaking, he could not have taken this city." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** "How utterly FOOLISH for men to exert themselves for what goes up in smoke, or to exhaust themselves for nothingness!" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 59 — *"This is the message that Jeremiah the prophet gave to the quartermaster Seraiah son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, when he went to Babylon with King Zedekiah of Judah in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign."*

**Traditional reading:** This dates the event to approximately 594–593 BC. Seraiah was the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe (Jeremiah 32:12). His title, translated "quartermaster" (KJV "quiet prince," margin "prince of rest"), means "prince of the resting-place" (Keil) — the royal official in charge of selecting overnight stopping-places for the king's entourage. Zedekiah's trip to Babylon was likely to reaffirm his vassal loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar after a rebellion attempt.

**Older commentaries (Keil & Delitzsch, via Biblehub):** Seraiah's title (שַׂר מְנוּחָה) does not mean "a peaceful prince" or "quiet prince," but "prince of the resting-place" — the king's quartermaster-general. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/51-64.htm

**Anglican (Church Pulpit Commentary):** Suggests "this journey of Zedekiah was the occasion of the prophecy against Babylon. For homage, if not the only object, was certainly one of the objects of the journey, and it therefore involved a deep disgrace to the theocracy. How fitting it was that the prophet should make use of this journey to furnish the medal with an appropriate reverse." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 60 — *"Jeremiah had written on a single scroll about all the disaster that would come upon Babylon—all these words that had been written concerning Babylon."*

**Traditional reading:** Jeremiah compiled the prophecies against Babylon (chapters 50–51, or the substance of them) onto a single scroll. Matthew Henry notes the value of having the word committed to writing: "It is of great advantage both to the propagating and to the perpetuating of the word of God to have it written." The parenthetical nature of this verse (Keil) sets up the charge that follows.

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** "Jeremiah wrote in a book all these words that are here written against Babylon. He received this notice that he might give it to all whom it might concern." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 61 — *"And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, 'When you get to Babylon, see that you read all these words aloud...'"*

**Traditional reading:** Seraiah is commissioned to read the scroll publicly upon arrival in Babylon. Constable takes the view that the reading was public, intended for Babylon itself (like Jonah's mission to Nineveh). Keil takes the view that the reading was not necessarily to Babylonians in a public assembly, but to proclaim God's word "on the very spot" as a prelude to the symbolic act. The Hebrew phrase "see to it, and read" (Keil) means "keep it in your eye, in your mind, that you read" — not "seek a good opportunity."

**Older commentaries (Keil):** "The reading was not intended to warn the Babylonians of the destruction threatened them, but was merely to be a proclamation of the word of the Lord against Babylon, on the very spot, for the purpose of connecting with it the symbolic action." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/51-64.htm

---

## v. 62 — *"...and say, 'O LORD, You have promised to cut off this place so that no one will remain—neither man nor beast. Indeed, it will be desolate forever.'"*

**Traditional reading:** After reading, Seraiah is to pray, reminding God of His own word — essentially saying, "You have said it; now do it." Ellicott calls this "of the nature of an implied prayer, reminding Jehovah of that which He had promised, and entreating him to fulfil it." Matthew Henry: "Though Seraiah sees Babylon flourishing, having read this prophecy he must foresee Babylon falling, and by virtue of it must curse its habitation, though it be taking root."

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** "When we have been reading the word of God it becomes us to direct to him whose word it is a humble believing acknowledgment of the truth, equity, and goodness, of what we have read." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 63 — *"When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates."*

**Traditional reading:** This is a symbolic prophetic action (like Jeremiah's linen belt in 13:1-7, the potter's vessel in 19:10, and the yokes in 27:2). The stone ensures the scroll sinks immediately and cannot be recovered — signifying that Babylon's fall is irreversible. Ellicott notes that "the parchment roll by itself might have floated, and been picked up and read, and so the stone was tied to it that it might sink at once." Gill adds that the scroll was cast "into the midst of the river, where the waters were deepest, and from whence it could not be taken up." Revelation 18:21 directly alludes to this action: a mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea.

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The symbolic act declares "that, in this manner, Babylon will sink (her power exhausted) and never rise again — because of the judgment Jehovah is bringing upon her sin." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-51.html

---

## v. 64 — *"Then you are to say, 'In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again, because of the disaster I will bring upon her. And her people will grow weary.'" Here end the words of Jeremiah.*

**Traditional reading:** Seraiah's spoken words explain the symbolism. "Never rise again" means permanent, irreversible ruin. "Her people will grow weary" (identical to the ending of v. 58) means the Babylonians would be utterly exhausted, unable to recover their strength. 

**"Thus far are the words of Jeremiah":** This editorial note (likely from Baruch or another compiler) signals that chapter 52 is a historical appendix taken largely from 2 Kings, not Jeremiah's own prophetic writing. Ellicott: "The words are clearly of the nature of what we should call an editorial note by the compiler of Jeremiah's prophecies, Baruch or another. He is careful to inform his readers that the narrative that follows in Jeremiah 52 was not written by Jeremiah." The Cambridge Bible notes that "and they shall be weary" was probably taken accidentally from v. 58 when the compiler transferred the closing formula to this later verse. The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Book of Jeremiah once ended with chapter 51.

**Older commentaries (Cambridge Bible):** The words "and they shall be weary" were "doubtless taken, probably by accident, from Jeremiah 51:58, when, on the addition of this short section by the compiler, the words 'Thus far … Jeremiah' were transferred to this later v." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/51-64.htm

**Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke cites Herodotus for a similar symbolic act by the Phocaeans, who threw a mass of iron into the sea and swore never to return until it rose and swam — a parallel ancient Near Eastern practice. He also notes that chapter 52 "is not the work of this prophet: it is not his style…It is merely historical." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-51.html

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Theological Emphases

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** Emphasises God's total sovereignty: Babylon was God's "battle-axe" and "golden cup" to judge the nations, yet is itself judged for its pride, idolatry, and cruelty. God uses sinful instruments and then holds them accountable. Henry underscores that "those that have carried all before them a great while will yet at length meet with their match, and their day also will come to fall."

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke):** Consistent emphasis on the literal-historical fulfillment via Cyrus and the Medes, with detailed citations from Herodotus and other classical sources. Also strong on moral application — Babylon fell "in consequence of its crimes." Clarke sees mystical Babylon (papal Rome of Revelation) as the ultimate referent.

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasises the certainty of divine judgment and the call to separation ("flee from Babylon"). Views the passage as a warning against worldliness. The symbolic act of sinking the scroll prefigures Revelation 18:21.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasises dual fulfillment — partial in the Medo-Persian conquest (~539 BC) and ultimate in the eschatological fall of "Babylon the Great" (Revelation 17–18). Stresses application for believers to "not put their trust, confidence, and resources into a kingdom that would be judged and conquered."

**Anglican (Church Pulpit Commentary):** Draws an extended typological parallel: "In every age of the world Babylon has had its counterpart.…Over against Jerusalem, Babylon…over against the New Jerusalem, Babylon the Great." The sinking of Seraiah's scroll prefigures the angel with the millstone in Revelation 18.

**Modern scholarship (Constable, Peake's):** Constable notes the premillennial vs. amillennial debate on whether Babylon must be literally rebuilt and destroyed again, or whether the language is hyperbolic for Medo-Persian conquest with spiritual fulfillment. Peake's notes textual difficulties (LXX omissions, the repetition of "and they shall be weary" as a scribal error from v. 58).
